title: Bidirectional BFS vs Oslo streets—who finds it?
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS race from start and goal across a street-graph until the frontiers meet. The visualization shows how meeting in the middle drastically reduces explored nodes compared to a one-way BFS.
ig_caption:
🚦 Oslo’s old streets meet a graph-search showdown! In this reel, **Bidirectional BFS** launches two breadth-first searches at once: one from the **start node** and one from the **goal node**. 🧠

In graph theory terms, your road network is a graph where intersections are vertices and streets are edges. Classic BFS explores outward level-by-level from one side, but **Bidirectional BFS** expands both frontiers simultaneously and stops the moment they intersect—often cutting the search space from ~O(b^d) to something closer to ~O(b^(d/2)) in many practical cases (b = branching factor, d = path length). ⚡

📍On a real street-map style graph like Gamlebyen’s layout, that “meet-in-the-middle” behavior turns an expensive route search into a focused exploration. Want the shortest path? This is the technique that makes the map feel faster. ✅

👉 Watch the frontier waves collide, then **comment “MAP”** and I’ll share the exact setup (graph model + visualization steps).
fb_caption:
🚍 Oslo (Gamlebyen) street map + a faster shortest-path search! In this visualization, **Bidirectional BFS** treats the map as a graph (intersections = nodes, roads = edges) and searches from both the start and destination until the two frontiers meet. 

📘 Why it matters: compared to regular BFS, it typically explores far fewer nodes because it reduces the effective depth each search must cover. 

👍 Like, share with a fellow coder, and comment your favorite part of the frontier collision!
yt_description:
Bidirectional BFS visualization on a real-world style street graph in Oslo (Gamlebyen)! 🗺️ Two BFS frontiers expand from start + goal, and the algorithm halts as soon as they intersect—showing why meeting in the middle is so powerful. 

Shorts keywords: bidirectional bfs, pathfinding, graph search, shortest path, breadth first search, algorithms, coding visualization, real map.

How it works (fast):
1) Build graph from intersections/roads
2) Run BFS from start and goal simultaneously
3) When frontiers meet, reconstruct the shortest path

Watch the frontier waves collide and tell me: should we add A* next? 🔥
